headline: Macy's moved the parade to Saturday. First time ever.
summary: Macy's postponed its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, with the balloons already being inflated. A nor'easter is due to hit New York on Thursday with gusts to 60 mph, and the giant balloons cannot fly in that. The parade skipped 1942 to 1944 for the war but had never been put off by weather. NBC will air last year's instead.

cover_question.q: Why not fly the balloons lower?

cover_answer: They did in 2019. The rule stops at 34 mph gusts.
table_question: If the big day might be dangerous, do you move it or risk it?

5-7.script: The giant balloon parade in New York isn't on today. A big windstorm is coming, and a balloon as big as a house could get blown into a lamppost. So Macy's moved the parade to Saturday, and TV shows last year's today. The balloons are folded up in a warehouse, waiting.
5-7.why: Moved, not cancelled, is the whole story. The balloons are waiting. A five-year-old hears 'no parade' as gone for good; Saturday is a day they can count to.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and what is in front of them is a parade that was promised and is not on. So the script gives one picture, a balloon as big as a house meeting a lamppost, and one fact to hold: the balloons are folded up and waiting. Expect 'can we watch it Saturday?' Yes, 8:30 in the morning.

8-12.script: The parade has a wind rule, like a lifeguard's flag at the pool: balloons stay down if gusts pass 34 mph. It came after 1997, when wind pushed a balloon into a lamppost and badly hurt a woman. Thursday's forecast says gusts to 60. So the 100th parade moves to Saturday, the first postponement ever.
8-12.why: Rule, reason, forecast, call. A chain they can check for themselves.
8-12.why_long: A child this age is working out how rules get made and whether adults follow them. The story hands over the chain: a woman hurt in 1997, a number written down afterwards, a forecast that beats the number, a decision that follows. The lifeguard's flag is the familiar version. Expect 'who made the rule?' The city, in 1998.

13-17.script: Why not fly the balloons lower, like 2019? The rule grounds them above 34 mph gusts, and the forecast says 60, so there was no middle setting. Second: the balloons were already going up when Macy's called it. Caution, or hoping the forecast would change?
13-17.why: A safety rule and a late call, both true. Teenagers can hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the wind rule left no room, and Macy's waited until the balloons were going up to say so. The script hands them 2019, 34 and 60, then asks about timing, the question the adults were asking too. Expect 'would they have flown if NBC had nothing to show?' I don't know. Nobody has said.

5-7.a: No. They're being emptied and kept in a warehouse in New Jersey until Saturday morning.

8-12.q: Why can't they just hold the ropes tighter?
8-12.a: A 1997 balloon hit a lamppost and hurt a woman. Over 34 mph gusts, no flying.
Not for weather. It skipped 1942 to 1944; the helium went to the war.

13-17.q: Why not fly the balloons lower?
13-17.a: They did in 2019. The rule grounds them above 34 mph gusts; the forecast says 60.
The NYPD has the final say on the balloons. Macy's and the city called it together.
